title: ANV Group to Acquire Open Lending for $3.15 a Share, About $372 Million, in an All-Cash Tender Offer at a 78% Premium
summary: ANV Group Holdings, a Blackstone-backed MGA platform, agreed to take auto-lending specialist Open Lending private for $3.15 per share, valuing it at about $372 million, with closing expected in Q3 2026.
description:
A Blackstone-backed insurance platform has agreed to buy a struggling auto-lending technology company. ANV Group Holdings has agreed to acquire Open Lending in an all-cash tender offer valuing the company at about $372 million, according to Insurance Business. The price is $3.15 per share, which the report says is a premium of roughly 78% to Open Lending's 90-day volume-weighted average share price as of June 15. Open Lending's board unanimously approved the deal. This article summarises that report and the company announcement. An earlier version of this article put the value of the deal at $1.3 billion. The reports we reviewed give about $372 million, so the figure has been corrected. Readers should check the companies' filings for the latest status of the tender offer.

What are the terms? The offer is all cash and structured as a tender offer, in which the buyer invites shareholders to sell their shares directly. Closing is expected in the third quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. After closing, Open Lending would be taken private and delisted from Nasdaq. The Insurance Business article does not mention shareholder support agreements or the minimum number of shares that must be tendered, so we do not describe those conditions. Open Lending's advisers were Financial Technology Partners as financial adviser and Jones Day as legal adviser. ANV's advisers were Evercore and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton and Garrison.

Who is the buyer? ANV Group is a Blackstone-backed managing general agent (MGA) platform. An MGA is a firm that underwrites insurance on behalf of insurers under delegated authority. ANV was formed in December 2025 from a transaction between AmTrust Financial Services and Blackstone Credit and Insurance. It took over seven AmTrust subsidiaries covering cyber excess and surplus lines, directors and officers liability, professional indemnity, mortgage and structured credit, and other lines in the US, UK and Continental Europe. AmTrust retained a significant equity interest and a ten-year capacity agreement. ANV added Iris Insurance Brokers in March 2026. Adam Karkowsky is chairman and chief executive. He said the deal directly advances the group's insurance-backed credit strategy, and that the company sees significant value creation ahead.

What does Open Lending do? Open Lending has operated for 25 years and provides loan analytics, risk-based pricing, risk modelling and default insurance to US auto lenders, mainly through its Lenders Protection programme. In plain terms, it helps lenders such as credit unions and banks make auto loans to borrowers who might otherwise be declined, by using its analytics and arranging insurance that protects the lender if the borrower defaults.

Why was the premium so large? The share price had been low. The report says the stock traded below $2.00 for much of 2025 and early 2026. A premium of 78% over the 90-day average therefore lifts the price to $3.15, but from a depressed base. The company's recent results explain the weakness. Revenue fell to $24.0 million in 2024 from $117.5 million in 2023, largely because of negative profit-share adjustments tied to higher-than-modelled defaults. Certified loans facilitated fell 25.9% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2025, and the stock dropped about 9% after hours following those results. Profit-share adjustments reflect revenue the company records based on its expectation of how loans will perform, so when defaults are higher than expected, the adjustments reduce revenue.

What are the risks and questions? First, regulatory approvals: the closing depends on them, and the article does not say which regulators. Second, integration and strategy: the buyer says Open Lending fits an insurance-backed credit strategy, but the report does not describe plans for the business or its employees. Third, credit performance: defaults on auto loans, particularly in the subprime segment, drive the economics of the business. A buyer that already operates in credit-linked insurance may be better placed to absorb that volatility than a listed company with a share price under pressure, though that is our observation and not a claim by the companies.

What does it mean for shareholders and lenders? Shareholders who tender receive $3.15 per share in cash. The offer gives them an exit at a price above recent trading, though some may feel it undervalues the company's long-term prospects; the report does not give shareholder reactions. For lenders using the programme, nothing changes immediately, and any changes would depend on the buyer's plans after closing.

How does this fit a wider trend? Private capital continues to buy and build insurance-related platforms, a theme that Deloitte's 2026 insurance M&A outlook, covered on this site, describes as private capital flowing into specialty lines and managing general agents. Blackstone's involvement through ANV is an example.

Readers should also note what the reports leave out: the amount of debt financing, the buyer's plans for Open Lending's management, and any break fee. None is given in the report we reviewed, and this article does not speculate about them.

This article summarises company and press reports and is not investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business and Open Lending announcement
image_alt: Insurance-backed lending and fintech acquisition deal (illustrative)
key_points: ANV Group Holdings agreed to acquire Open Lending through an all-cash tender offer at $3.15 per share, valuing the company at about $372 million; the board approved it unanimously.
The price is a premium of roughly 78% to Open Lending's 90-day volume-weighted average price as of June 15.
Closing is expected in Q3 2026, subject to regulatory approvals, after which Open Lending would be taken private and delisted from Nasdaq.
ANV is a Blackstone-backed MGA platform formed in December 2025 from a transaction between AmTrust Financial Services and Blackstone Credit and Insurance; Adam Karkowsky is chairman and CEO.
Open Lending provides loan analytics, risk-based pricing and default insurance to US auto lenders; revenue fell to $24.0 million in 2024 from $117.5 million in 2023.
why_it_matters: Auto lenders use default insurance and analytics to lend to borrowers with weaker credit. The deal shows private capital buying into insurance-backed lending after a difficult stretch for the target.

title: IRDAI Proposes Rules for How It Makes Rules: 21-Day Consultation, Three-Year Reviews and Cost-Benefit Assessment
summary: India's insurance regulator published a draft on June 17, 2026 setting a formal procedure for making regulations and issuing subsidiary instructions, with at least 21 days of public comment and a review of every regulation every three years; comments were due by July 8.
description:
India's insurance regulator has proposed a rulebook for its own rule-making. On June 17, 2026, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) put out a draft regulation setting out the procedure for making regulations and issuing subsidiary instructions, with comments invited until July 8, 2026. The draft rests on the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, which changed the Insurance Act, 1938 and related laws and, according to Indian reports, took effect for most provisions in February 2026. This article summarises the draft as reported by Business Standard and by tax and legal commentary. The draft's full text was not reviewed for this update, so readers should consult IRDAI's website for the exact wording and any final version. An earlier version of this article is superseded by this one.

What problem is the draft trying to solve? Regulators across the world make rules, and the quality of those rules depends on how they are made. A regulator that consults early, explains its reasoning and reviews old rules tends to produce regulations that industry can implement and that consumers can trust. IRDAI already consulted stakeholders on many drafts, but the process was not set out in one regulation. The draft would codify those practices and add duties, which is what the reports mean by greater structure, transparency and accountability. The Tax Corp lists the guiding principles as policyholder protection, orderly industry growth, service quality and trust, transparency, proportionality and accountability, ease of doing business, use of technology and adoption of best practices.

What would be published, and for how long? Under the draft, IRDAI would put draft regulations on its website with a statement of particulars. Business Standard reports that this statement would cover the statutory provisions invoked, the regulatory intent and, where applicable, relevant global best practices. The minimum period for public comment from insurers, intermediaries and other stakeholders would be 21 days. In this case the window from June 17 to July 8 is exactly 21 days.

How must IRDAI respond to comments? The draft requires IRDAI to publish a general statement explaining how it responded to comments by the date a regulation is notified. That does not oblige the regulator to accept any particular suggestion, but it requires an explanation of the overall treatment. If the final regulation differs substantially from the draft for reasons other than stakeholder feedback, IRDAI would have to consult again. This protects the public from a change late in the process that nobody had the chance to examine.

What is the cost-benefit assessment? Before finalising a regulation, IRDAI would assess the expected costs and benefits for policyholders, the insurance industry and the broader economy. The reports do not describe the method or whether the assessment would be published. A cost-benefit exercise can be simple or detailed, and the value of the requirement will depend on the standard IRDAI sets for itself.

How often would regulations be reviewed? All regulations would be reviewed every three years from publication, unless an earlier review, amendment or repeal is needed. Periodic review matters in insurance because markets change quickly. Rules written for paper-based distribution may fit poorly with digital sales, and rules written when foreign ownership was capped may need updating now that India has opened insurance to 100% foreign investment, as reported in separate coverage on this site.

What are subsidiary instructions and committees? Beyond formal regulations, IRDAI issues circulars, guidelines and other instructions. The Tax Corp says the Act creates a formal regime for them and that consultative committees advise the regulator. According to Business Standard, the committees would include external experts in insurance, finance, law and information technology, plus industry representatives and regulator officials. Their recommendations would be advisory and would not be binding on IRDAI.

Is there an exception for urgent matters? Yes. IRDAI could skip the consultation or committee steps in urgent public-interest cases, provided it records its reasons in writing. Such exceptions are common in regulatory frameworks, because delay can itself harm consumers, for example when a firm's solvency is at risk. They also create a point of scrutiny: the more often the exception is used, the weaker the consultation commitment becomes. The requirement to record reasons gives courts, industry and the public a document to examine.

Who is affected? Insurers, reinsurers, brokers, third-party administrators, surveyors and other intermediaries all fall under IRDAI's regulations. Consumer groups and policyholders can also comment. Larger firms generally have the resources to respond to drafts; smaller firms and individual policyholders do not, so how IRDAI publicises drafts and presents them in plain language will affect who is heard.

What should readers watch for? Four things stand out: whether IRDAI finalises the regulation in the form proposed; whether the 21-day minimum is treated as a floor or a norm; how detailed the published cost-benefit assessments are; and how often the urgency exception is used. Another point is timing. The Act's wider rule-making programme requires IRDAI to prepare new regulations, so the quality of the consultation procedure will be tested quickly.

This article is a summary of press and legal commentary and is not legal advice. Refer to IRDAI's official publications for the draft and any final regulation.
source_name: Business Standard and The Tax Corp
image_alt: Indian insurance regulation and policy framework consultation (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI proposed the draft on June 17, 2026, titled as a procedure for making regulations and subsidiary instructions, under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025; comments were due by July 8, 2026.
Draft regulations would be published with a statement of particulars covering the statutory provisions used, the intent and relevant global best practice, with at least 21 days for public comment.

IRDAI would publish a general statement on how it handled comments by the date of notification, and consult again if the final rule differs substantially from the draft for reasons other than feedback.
Every regulation would be reviewed every three years from publication, and IRDAI would assess expected costs and benefits for policyholders, industry and the wider economy before finalising.
Consultative committees on subsidiary instructions would be advisory and non-binding, and IRDAI could skip consultation in urgent public-interest cases if it records written reasons.
why_it_matters: Insurers, brokers and policyholders gain a predictable route to comment on rules that affect them. The urgency exemption and the advisory status of committees show where discretion would remain with the regulator.

title: PwC's 2026 Midyear Outlook: 191 Insurance Deals Worth Almost $30 Billion in Six Months, With AI Dividing Investors
summary: PwC counted 191 disclosed insurance transactions worth almost $30 billion from December 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, slightly below the prior six months, and says uncertainty over AI is lowering broker valuations and raising deal scrutiny.
description:
Insurance dealmaking is still active, but artificial intelligence is making investors rethink what insurance businesses are worth. That is the message of PwC's 2026 midyear deals outlook for insurance, as reported by Digital Insurance on June 23, 2026. According to the report, PwC counted 191 disclosed insurance sector transactions worth almost $30 billion between December 1, 2025 and May 31, 2026. In the previous period, ending November 30, 2025, there were 207 deals worth nearly $32 billion, so both volume and value fell slightly. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article said that deal appetite remained strong because of AI, which overstates PwC's position. PwC describes the drivers of dealmaking as healthy but says AI is creating uncertainty that has tightened scrutiny and lowered some valuations, and the article now reflects that. We reviewed only the Digital Insurance report, not the full PwC document.

What are the numbers? The count covers disclosed transactions in the insurance sector over six months. The drop from 207 deals to 191 is about 8% by number, and the fall in value from nearly $32 billion to almost $30 billion is about 6%, which we calculated from the figures PwC gave. These are small changes, consistent with PwC's view that the market is steady and not frozen. The report does not break the numbers down by type of business or region.

What is driving deals? PwC says strategic and financial deal drivers remain healthy. Higher premium rates, loss cost inflation and better underwriting have been improving profitability across insurance lines, and investors remain interested in the sector. Higher profitability gives insurers and brokers more capital to buy other companies and makes the sector attractive to private capital. This matches Deloitte's 2026 outlook, covered on this site, which expects a disciplined and selective M&A market.

Why is AI a source of uncertainty? The report says investors are divided. One view is that AI could let new entrants undercut broker commissions, because a technology company might be able to place insurance more cheaply than a traditional broker. The opposite view is that AI could reduce brokerage costs through greater efficiency and accuracy, which would support margins for established firms. Which view proves right matters for how much buyers are willing to pay for brokers, MGAs and other distribution businesses. Mark Friedman, PwC's insurance deals leader and a co-author of the report, said that 2026 has seen uncertainty over how AI may disrupt the sector. He linked this to tougher deal scrutiny and lower valuations of publicly traded brokers.

Could AI also increase deals? PwC suggests it could. Many insurers and reinsurers are investing in AI for underwriting, claims and workflow automation. If those investments raise performance, valuations and M&A activity could rise, since buyers may pay for technology and data capabilities, and since firms may merge to gain scale in technology spending. The report does not forecast how much, and PwC frames the point as a possibility.

How does this connect to other developments? On this site, Sixfold's AI Underwriter launch, covered in a separate article, is an example of vendors selling AI directly to carriers, with vendor-reported gains in processing speed. Lockton's fiscal 2026 results, also covered here, show a large private broker growing 12% while saying it sees AI as an accelerator of human expertise. Those examples illustrate both sides of the investor debate without settling it.

What should different readers take from this? For insurers and brokers considering a sale, the message is that valuations are being influenced by views about AI, so a clear story about technology and client relationships may matter. For buyers, the scrutiny means more diligence on how exposed a target is to disintermediation. For customers, M&A can bring changes in service, products or ownership, though existing contracts normally continue. For investors, the report is a reminder that sector sentiment can shift quickly with technology narratives.

What are the limits of the data? Counts of disclosed deals leave out private transactions that were not announced. Deal values are often estimates, and the report as covered does not state a methodology. PwC itself advises companies on transactions, so its outlook should be read with that in mind.

What should readers watch next? The next PwC update will show whether deal counts continue to drift lower or recover, and whether broker valuations stabilise. Large strategic deals, such as Zurich's takeover of Beazley covered elsewhere on this site, show that major transactions are still possible even when the overall count dips. The balance between those large deals and smaller tuck-ins will shape how the market looks to customers.

How should customers think about this? Most policyholders will not notice an acquisition directly, since contracts continue. But a broker or insurer owned by a larger group may change its services, fees or panel of insurers over time. Businesses can ask their broker about ownership, how it is paid and whether its technology changes affect service.

This article summarises a press report of a consulting outlook and is not investment advice.
source_name: PwC US Deals 2026 midyear outlook (via Digital Insurance, June 23, 2026)
image_alt: Artificial intelligence and insurance technology mergers and acquisitions (illustrative)
key_points: From December 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, PwC counted 191 disclosed insurance transactions worth almost $30 billion, against 207 deals worth nearly $32 billion in the prior six months.
PwC says strategic and financial deal drivers remain healthy, with higher rates, loss cost inflation and better underwriting improving profitability, and investors still interested in the sector.
Investors are divided on AI: it could let new entrants undercut broker commissions, or lower brokerage costs through efficiency and accuracy.
Many insurers and reinsurers are investing in AI for underwriting, claims and workflow automation, which PwC suggests could raise valuations and M&A activity.
Mark Friedman, PwC's insurance deals leader, said '2026 has seen uncertainty over how AI may disrupt the sector', linking it to tougher scrutiny and lower publicly traded broker valuations.
why_it_matters: Mergers and acquisitions decide which companies insure, broker and hold customers' money. PwC's data show that dealmaking is steady but being re-priced for the risk that AI changes how insurance is sold.

title: UAE's New Central Bank Law Sets a September 2026 Reconciliation Deadline for Banks, Insurers and Fintechs
summary: Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 consolidated UAE banking and insurance regulation under the Central Bank, widened the regulatory perimeter to technology platforms and gave regulated firms a one-year transition ending in mid-September 2026.
description:
The United Arab Emirates rewrote the legal foundations of its financial sector in 2025, and regulated firms were given a fixed period to catch up. Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, known as the Central Bank Law, came into force on September 16, 2025. It repealed the earlier Central Bank legislation of 2018 and the standalone insurance law, Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023, and placed banking, payments, open finance and insurance regulation under one statute administered by the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE). This article is based on published analyses by the law firms Norton Rose Fulbright and Hadef & Partners. An earlier version of this article described some details more loosely than those sources do, so the figures below follow the firms' own wording, and where they differ, that is noted. It is general information and not legal advice.

What does the law do? The law consolidates regulation that had been spread across several instruments. Insurance, which was moved under the central bank in 2020 when the former Insurance Authority was merged into it, no longer sits in a standalone statute. The same regulator now supervises banks, payment providers, insurers and other licensed financial institutions under one framework, with powers to examine and, where needed, penalise.

What is the reconciliation deadline? Article 184 gives persons subject to the law one year from commencement to reconcile their positions with its requirements. Norton Rose Fulbright gives the end of that period as September 16, 2026, while Hadef & Partners refers to 15 September 2026 under Article 184. The one-day difference reflects different ways of counting the year; firms should rely on the Central Bank's own statements. Both firms note that the Central Bank's board may extend the period where appropriate, and Hadef & Partners reported that no general extension had been announced at the time of its article. Because that date has now passed, readers should check the CBUAE website for any extension or guidance issued since, and this article does not say whether any firm has been found non-compliant.

What is the new regulatory perimeter? Article 61 lists activities that require a licence, including deposit-taking, credit and funding, open finance, money transfer, virtual-asset payment services, stored-value and digital money services, and certain promotion or marketing of licensed activities. Article 62 adds that using a particular technology or business model does not by itself take an activity outside the perimeter. According to the law firms, this expressly captures certain virtual-asset payment tokens, decentralised finance, platforms, decentralised applications and supporting technological infrastructure. For insurers, the practical meaning is that insurtech platforms and technology providers that enable regulated activity should check whether they now need authorisation.

What are the penalties? Norton Rose Fulbright says the law raises the maximum administrative fine from AED 200 million to AED 1 billion, a fivefold increase. Hadef & Partners separately reports that carrying on licensed financial activities without the required licence or authorisation can bring imprisonment and fines from AED 50,000 to AED 500 million. These are different penalty regimes, one administrative and one criminal, which explains why two different headline numbers appear in commentary. Article 181 also allows personal consequences for responsible management where their knowledge, negligence or failure to perform duties is established, which means senior managers cannot assume that liability stops with the company.

What about existing contracts? Hadef & Partners points to Article 132, under which Central Bank regulations are not retroactive and do not stop agreements made before they were issued from being carried out. Existing loan, security and other finance documents are not invalidated or required to be re-executed. The firm describes the reconciliation deadline as a compliance date, not a date after which existing arrangements lapse.

What obligations apply to insurers? Norton Rose Fulbright notes that the law introduces specific obligations on licensed institutions, including insurance companies. They must have fraud prevention and detection systems, notify customers promptly of breaches or fraud and take immediate corrective action to limit harm. Several 2026 regulations apply as well, according to Hadef & Partners: C1/2026 on operational risk and operational resilience, issued in February 2026; C4/2026, the Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, also from February 2026, which covers branches of foreign insurers and the opening of branches and subsidiaries; C5/2026, a remuneration regulation for banks and insurance companies effective April 2026; and C3/2026, a telemarketing regulation effective March 31, 2026. The Central Bank has also issued guidance on the responsible use of artificial intelligence and machine learning by licensed institutions.

What should firms be doing? Practical steps include mapping every activity against Articles 61 and 62 to confirm whether a licence is needed; reviewing board and management responsibilities in light of Article 181; checking that fraud detection and customer notification processes meet the new duties; aligning remuneration structures with C5/2026; and documenting the reconciliation work so that it can be shown to the regulator. Foreign insurers with branches in the UAE should also review C4/2026.

What is not yet clear? The sources do not say how the Central Bank will treat firms that miss the deadline, whether it will grant extensions to individual firms, or how it will apply the new fine ceiling in practice. Nor do they quantify how many firms are affected. Until the regulator publishes enforcement guidance, the size of the penalty increase tells readers about the ceiling, not about likely outcomes.

Why does it matter beyond the UAE? The UAE positions itself as a regional hub for insurance, banking and fintech. A single, broader regulatory framework with explicit coverage of digital assets and platforms signals to international firms how the country intends to supervise new business models. Companies weighing whether to base operations there will want to read the underlying law and the CBUAE's regulations rather than rely on summaries.

This article is a summary of third-party legal commentary, not legal advice. Firms should take advice from UAE counsel and confirm current requirements with the Central Bank of the UAE.
source_name: Norton Rose Fulbright and Hadef & Partners
image_alt: UAE financial district and central bank regulation (illustrative)
key_points: Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 came into force on September 16, 2025, replacing the 2018 Central Bank law and the 2023 insurance law (Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023).
Persons subject to the law have a one-year period to reconcile their positions; law firms give the end date as September 15 or 16, 2026, and the Central Bank's board may extend it.

The perimeter now expressly covers open finance, virtual-asset payment services and technology platforms, with Article 62 saying a technology or business model does not by itself put an activity outside the law.

Norton Rose Fulbright says the maximum administrative fine rises from AED 200 million to AED 1 billion; Hadef & Partners reports criminal fines of AED 50,000 to AED 500 million for unlicensed activity.
2026 Central Bank regulations already issued include operational resilience (C1/2026), insurance company licensing (C4/2026) and remuneration (C5/2026).
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and fintechs operating in the UAE answer to a single, wider regulator with larger penalties. Firms that missed the reconciliation window face questions about licensing and personal liability for managers.

title: US Auto Insurance in 2026: The Zebra Projects $2,256 and Rises in 19 States, While Insurify Forecasts a 1% Increase to $2,158
summary: Two forecasts for 2026 differ in level but agree prices are flattening after the post-pandemic spike: The Zebra projects an average $2,256 with increases in 19 states, and Insurify forecasts a 1% rise to $2,158 with tariffs and repair costs as wildcards.
description:
Car insurance prices in the United States are no longer rising at the pace of the post-pandemic spike, but forecasters disagree on how much they will move in 2026 and where. This article compares two published outlooks: The Zebra's 2026 State of Insurance: Auto report, released on January 13, 2026, and an Insurify forecast reported by Insurance Journal on February 3, 2026. An earlier version of this article attributed weather exposure to The Zebra's outlook and treated both reports as if they described the same measure. We could not confirm the weather attribution in the sources, and the two reports use different data, so the figures below are labelled by source. This is general information and not insurance advice.

What does The Zebra project? The Zebra, an insurance comparison site, projects that the typical American driver will pay an average of $2,256 a year in 2026. It expects premiums to rise in 19 states and fall in 13 during the first two quarters of 2026. The company's press release names only some states. It lists Oregon, Maryland and Utah among states with increases of 8% to 21%, and Vermont, Minnesota and Mississippi among those with decreases of 6% to 13%. The report analyses more than 32 million auto insurance rates across all 34,500 US ZIP codes, covering 11 years, using the company's own Dynamic Insurance Rating Tool. The Zebra's chief commercial officer, David Seider, said Americans face rising costs for various reasons and urged consumers to shop around and compare quotes.

What happened in 2025? The Zebra says average premiums rose about 3% nationally from 2024 to 2025, down from an 18% jump the year before. It reports that six states saw increases above 50% over that period: Louisiana, Nevada, New York, Georgia, Maryland and Utah. It also says Americans spend 2.6% of annual income on auto insurance on average, with residents of Arkansas, Louisiana and Florida spending nearly 5%.

What does Insurify forecast? Insurify, another comparison and quoting platform, reported that the average full-coverage premium in 2025 was $2,144, down 6%, following an increase of about 46% from 2022 to 2024. For 2026 it forecasts a 1% rise to $2,158. State by state, 39 states saw price decreases in 2025, eight of them by at least 15%, and Wyoming, Iowa and Arkansas each cut average prices by more than 20%. New Jersey's average premium rose 20%, one of four jurisdictions with double-digit increases, and Washington, D.C. had the highest average annual cost at $4,017. For 2026, Insurify expects prices to rise in 35 states and fall in 15.

Why do the numbers differ? The two firms measure different things. Insurify's 2025 average is for full coverage, while The Zebra's projection is a typical driver average from its own rating tool and sample. Their state counts differ as well, because The Zebra's 19-and-13 counts cover the first half of 2026 while Insurify's 35-and-15 count covers the whole year. The Zebra's later report, linked from its press page, cites a median premium of $2,079 a year, which is yet another measure. Readers should therefore not conclude that one source is right and the other wrong; they are describing different baskets.

What risks do forecasters flag? Insurify says tariffs are a wildcard. Their effect on auto repair costs is not fully realised yet, and it says repair costs are likely to rise in 2026 because insurers have not yet passed these costs to consumers. Matt Brannon, a senior economic analyst at Insurify, said risks are compounding in crowded states that already have a high cost of living. Repair costs matter because insurers pay for parts and labour on collision and comprehensive claims, so higher costs for parts, whether from tariffs or supply, tend to feed into premiums with a lag.

Why were 2023 and 2024 so painful? Both reports refer to a period of historic increases following the pandemic. Insurify cites about 46% growth from 2022 to 2024 and The Zebra cites an 18% jump in the year before 2025. Insurers had faced higher claims costs and had to catch up on pricing. As claims costs moderated and rate increases earned through, some insurers began to compete for customers again, which is consistent with the falling prices Insurify observed in 39 states in 2025.

What should drivers do? Compare quotes from several insurers at renewal, because the price for the same driver can vary widely between companies. Review coverage levels and deductibles, and ask about discounts for bundling, safe driving programmes or low mileage. Check your credit-based insurance score where state law allows its use, and keep your record clean. The Zebra notes that texting while driving leads to an average 17% premium increase. If your premium rose sharply, ask your insurer to explain the factors and whether other rate classes apply.

What should we watch? Tariff decisions and repair cost indices, state regulatory decisions on rate filings, and whether the states forecast to rise in the first half do so. The Zebra's projection covers only the first half of 2026, so full-year outcomes remain to be seen.

This article compares two published forecasts and is not insurance advice. Premiums depend on individual circumstances, and the figures are averages.
source_name: The Zebra (Business Wire) and Insurify (Insurance Journal)
image_alt: Car insurance and US auto insurance premiums 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: The Zebra's 2026 State of Insurance: Auto report, released January 13, 2026, projects an average of $2,256 a year, with increases in 19 states and decreases in 13 in the first half of 2026.

The Zebra says average premiums rose about 3% from 2024 to 2025, after an 18% jump the year before; its named examples include Oregon, Maryland and Utah rising 8% to 21% and Vermont, Minnesota and Mississippi falling 6% to 13%.
Insurify, reported on February 3, 2026, put the 2025 average full-coverage premium at $2,144, down 6%, and forecasts a 1% rise to $2,158 in 2026, with prices rising in 35 states and falling in 15.
Insurify calls tariffs a wildcard because their effect on repair costs is not fully realised, and says insurers have not yet passed likely repair-cost increases on to consumers.

why_it_matters: Drivers who saw large increases in 2023 and 2024 may now find prices flat or falling in some states and rising in others. Shopping around is the main lever consumers control while repair costs and tariffs add uncertainty.
